title: Distributed Key-Value Store
oneLine: Partition by consistent hashing, replicate across failure domains, use configurable quorums, and reconcile replicas with versioning, gossip, hinted handoff, and Merkle trees.
opening: I would first decide whether the store is CP or AP for the target operations. For a Dynamo-style highly available store, keys are partitioned with consistent hashing and replicated to N nodes across failure domains. Reads and writes use configurable quorums R and W; choosing R + W greater than N creates overlap, but conflict handling and failure semantics still need to be defined. Each node uses a write-optimized LSM path—commit log, memtable, immutable SSTables—with Bloom filters and compaction for reads. Membership and liveness are distributed by gossip, temporary failures use hinted handoff, and background anti-entropy compares Merkle trees. Values carry versions such as vector clocks or logical timestamps so concurrent writes can be detected and reconciled rather than silently overwritten.
ask: What operations and maximum key/value sizes are required?
Is availability or linearizable consistency more important during partition?
What read/write latency and throughput are expected?
Must we support range scans, transactions, secondary indexes, TTL, or compare-and-set?
scale: Partition count should greatly exceed node count so ownership can move in small units.
Replication factor N=3 is a common starting point, but choose it from durability and failure-domain targets.
R and W are latency/consistency knobs; they do not remove the need for versioning and read repair.

decisions.default: Choose AP for carts/sessions/telemetry; choose CP for locks, uniqueness, and money-like invariants.
decisions.why: During a partition, accepting writes on both sides conflicts with a single authoritative order.
decisions.switch: Expose different consistency levels per operation when the product can tolerate the complexity.

decisions.default: N=3 with R/W tuned to read or write latency; use strong leader-based reads for truly linearizable operations.
decisions.why: Quorum overlap improves freshness but sloppy quorums and concurrent writes can still create conflicts.
decisions.switch: Local quorum per region for latency plus asynchronous cross-region replication when global strong consistency is unnecessary.

decisions.default: LSM tree for high write throughput and append-friendly durability.
decisions.why: Sequential writes and batching outperform random in-place updates at scale.
decisions.switch: B-tree engines fit read-heavy workloads with range scans and lower compaction pressure.

decisions.default: Detect concurrent versions and apply domain-specific merge or last-write only when acceptable.
decisions.why: Blind last-write-wins can lose valid updates and wall clocks can skew.
decisions.switch: Use CRDTs for mergeable counters/sets or a leader/consensus group for non-mergeable invariants.

deepDives.title: LSM mechanics
points: Acknowledge only after durable log policy is satisfied.
Flush sorted memtables to SSTables; Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain the key.
Compaction trades write amplification and I/O for bounded read amplification and reclaimed tombstones.

deepDives.title: Failure recovery
points: Sloppy quorum writes to healthy fallback nodes and stores a hint for the intended replica.
Hinted handoff repairs short outages; Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs long divergence.
Use repair throttling so recovery does not overload foreground traffic.

deepDives.title: Versioning
points: Vector clocks capture causality but metadata can grow; prune or use dotted versions.
Hybrid logical clocks provide sortable time with bounded physical-clock reliance.
Read repair must not overwrite a genuinely concurrent value without a resolution rule.

failures.response: Return/merge versions, apply domain reconciliation, or route the operation through a CP path.
Rate-limit compaction, isolate I/O, stagger jobs, and monitor write/read amplification.
Any node can coordinate, membership is gossiped, and ownership uses stable epochs/preference lists.
Use repair windows and garbage-collection grace periods so all replicas see deletions before tombstones are removed.

questions.q: Does R + W > N guarantee strong consistency?
questions.a: It guarantees quorum overlap under the assumed replica set, but not automatically linearizability—sloppy quorum, concurrent writes, stale topology, and conflict resolution still matter. A leader/consensus protocol is clearer for strict ordering.

questions.q: How do you add a node?
questions.a: Assign virtual-token ranges, stream data from current owners, serve through the old owner or dual-read during transfer, validate, then advance the ownership epoch.

questions.q: What is a Merkle tree used for?
questions.a: It compares hashes of key ranges so replicas identify divergent subranges without transferring the entire dataset, then repair only those ranges.
It can say a key is definitely absent or possibly present, avoiding unnecessary SSTable reads. False positives cost an extra lookup; false negatives are not allowed.

mistakes: Saying CAP means a system can only ever have two properties
Claiming quorum overlap alone gives exactly one version
seniorSignal: Separate client consistency, replication protocol, conflict semantics, and storage-engine mechanics. Explain how the system converges after failures without destroying foreground latency.
implementation: Cassandra/Dynamo-style reference for AP; etcd/Spanner-like consensus for CP
LSM concepts map to RocksDB/Cassandra storage engines
Java coordinator with async replica calls, deadlines, and per-key version metadata
Background repair jobs with token-range throttling and observability
